title: Review—Measurement and Analysis of Cancer Biomarkers Based on Electrochemical Biosensors

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Platforms and Device Architectures
subsections.subsection_title: Microfluidic, Multiplexed, and Point-of-Care Electrochemical Systems
subsections.content:
Microfluidic electrochemical biosystems are increasingly used to translate cancer biomarker assays from benchtop formats to compact, automated platforms with reduced reagent consumption, controlled mass transport, and shorter assay times. Early electrochemical microfluidic immunoarrays demonstrated high-throughput and multiplexed quantification of protein biomarkers by integrating patterned electrodes, microchannels, and nanostructured signal-amplification chemistries, thereby addressing the heterogeneity of cancer-associated analytes more effectively than single-marker tests ref [3], ref [10]. This systems-level trend has been reinforced by broader advances in nanomaterial-enabled electrochemical biosensors, which improve sensitivity while remaining compatible with miniaturized chip and cartridge architectures ref [9].

A key design direction is simultaneous measurement of biomarker panels rather than isolated targets. Microfluidic chips combining multiple gastric cancer biomarkers illustrate how multiplexing can improve early-stage diagnostic discrimination in clinically relevant samples ref [2]. Related array-based strategies are also motivated by the biological diversity of cancer markers, including cytokines, microRNAs, matrix metalloproteinases, and glycan-associated signatures ref [5], ref [7], ref [11], ref [12], ref [13], ref [14], ref [8]. In practice, multiplexing can be implemented through parallel electrodes, bead-based capture zones, barcode labels, or sequential fluid routing, but analytical gains depend on minimizing cross-talk, maintaining calibration across channels, and preserving specificity in complex matrices ref [3], ref [10].

For point-of-care deployment, screen-printed electrodes, magnetic beads, and disposable cartridges are especially attractive because they support low-cost fabrication and simple operation. An ultrasensitive TNF-α immunosensor using polymer-coated magnetic microparticles on a screen-printed gold electrode exemplifies this route toward saliva-based testing and decentralized analysis ref [1]. Integration of bead-based electrochemical immunosensors with automated microfluidics and even bioreactor interfaces further enables continual monitoring of cell-secreted biomarkers, extending use cases from diagnosis to therapy-response assessment and dynamic tumor biology studies ref [4]. Beyond proteins, miniaturized electrochemical platforms are being explored for volatile biomarkers and liquid-biopsy analytes such as circulating tumor DNA, indicating that future point-of-care systems will likely couple multiplexed electroanalysis with broader sample-to-answer workflows ref [19], ref [16], ref [18].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Platforms and Device Architectures
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Transduction Modes and Sensor Architecture Fundamentals
subsections.content:
Electrochemical cancer biosensors are fundamentally defined by the coupling between a biorecognition layer and an electrode transducer, with performance determined by interfacial electron transfer, double-layer structure, and mass transport. The main transduction modes are amperometric/voltammetric, potentiometric, conductometric/field-effect, and impedimetric readout, each emphasizing different aspects of the biointerface ref [20], ref [21], ref [22]. In practice, current-based methods offer high analytical sensitivity for redox-active labels or enzymatic amplification, whereas potentiometric and field-effect architectures are attractive for label-free detection through surface charge perturbation ref [18], ref [22].

Sensor architecture is therefore inseparable from transduction physics. Typical platforms use two- or three-electrode cells, where working-electrode material, surface nanostructuring, and immobilization chemistry govern signal magnitude and reproducibility. Gold, carbon, graphene-family materials, and metal nanostructures are widely used to increase electroactive area and facilitate functionalization, while self-assembled monolayers, polymer films, and protein lattices help orient capture probes and suppress nonspecific adsorption ref [19], ref [20], ref [22]. In miniaturized formats, integration with microfluidics improves diffusion control, lowers sample volume, and stabilizes interfacial conditions, but also makes channel geometry and electrode placement integral design variables ref [17].

Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy is especially important in cancer biomarker analysis because it can resolve binding-induced changes in charge-transfer resistance under faradaic conditions or capacitance/dielectric changes in non-faradaic operation, enabling label-free measurements of proteins, nucleic acids, cells, and vesicles ref [21]. Complementarily, field-effect transistor biosensors translate interfacial charge modulation into conductance shifts and can provide rapid, low-power readout, although ionic screening and surface functionalization remain central architectural constraints in physiological media ref [18]. Across all formats, the core design principle is to match the recognition element, electrode interface, and readout mode to the biomarker’s abundance, size, and transport properties to maximize clinical sensitivity and robustness ref [20], ref [22].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Platforms and Device Architectures
subsections.content:
Immunosensor and affinity-based electrochemical platforms remain central to cancer biomarker analysis because they combine molecular recognition with low-cost, miniaturizable transduction. Most formats use antibodies in direct, competitive, or sandwich configurations, while broader affinity interfaces include lectins, peptides, and molecularly imprinted receptors for targets that are difficult to address with conventional antibodies ref [26], ref [27], ref [28]. For serum protein markers, these architectures have been demonstrated for clinically relevant analytes such as AFP, PSA, CA 15-3, and matrix metalloproteinases, with electrochemical readout enabling operation in compact and potentially point-of-care formats ref [25], ref [29], ref [30], ref [33].

A major design trend is signal amplification. Electrochemical ELISA-type immunoassays increasingly incorporate nanostructured electrodes, enzyme-loaded carriers, redox-active nanocomposites, metal deposition, and stimulus-responsive materials to improve sensitivity and dynamic range ref [26], ref [31], ref [32]. Representative examples include conductometric AFP assays based on bienzyme-functionalized silica beads ref [25], peptide-assisted silver deposition for PSA detection ref [29], redox-active polyaniline derivative-Au/Pd labels for multiplexed immunoassay ref [31], and Ca2+-triggered alginate hydrogel precipitation for amplified impedimetric sensing ref [32]. Such strategies are especially valuable for early-stage cancer screening, where biomarkers may be present at ultralow abundance.

Affinity-based electrochemical sensing has also expanded beyond classical antigen-antibody recognition. Lectin biosensors support label-free glycoprofiling of cancer-associated glycoforms, adding specificity at the post-translational level that total-protein measurements may miss ref [24]. In parallel, molecular imprinting has emerged as a robust synthetic-recognition strategy for tumor markers, as illustrated by surface-imprinted sensing of pleural mesothelioma biomarkers and disposable imprinted-polymer detection of CA 15-3 ref [23], ref [30]. Collectively, these platforms show that future immunosensor design will likely emphasize multiplexing, antifouling interfaces, and validation in real clinical matrices to improve translational utility ref [27], ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Platforms and Device Architectures
subsections.subsection_title: Cell, Exosome, and In Vivo Electrochemical Sensing Platforms
subsections.content:
Electrochemical platforms for whole-cell analysis extend biomarker sensing from isolated molecules to functional phenotypes, including viability, adhesion, proliferation, invasion, and metabolic activity. Chronoamperometric assays on screen-printed electrodes have been used for rapid viability assessment in cell populations, highlighting the compatibility of low-cost electrode formats with routine cancer cell monitoring ref [34]. Label-free impedance systems are especially important because they transduce changes in cell attachment and morphology into dynamic electrical signatures, enabling real-time tracking of stromal regulation, migration, and invasion in colon cancer models ref [37]. Related bioimpedimetric approaches, when coupled with growth kinetics, can also discriminate differences in tumor aggressiveness, while 3D micro-array electrode designs and nanoparticle-assisted electrocatalytic formats improve capture efficiency and counting sensitivity for circulating or suspended tumor cells ref [36], ref [38], ref [39].

At the extracellular vesicle level, exosome-oriented electrochemical sensors have become a major liquid-biopsy architecture because they combine molecular specificity with minimally invasive sampling. Recent reviews of exosomal protein detection emphasize the growing use of antibody-, aptamer-, and nanomaterial-enabled electrochemical transduction for cancer screening, diagnosis, and prognosis ref [40]. Device performance is strongly shaped by interfacial nanoarchitecture: nanostructured capture surfaces with ex situ or in situ formed morphologies enhance vesicle immobilization and improve downstream electrochemical readout ref [41]. Integrated magneto-electrochemical systems further simplify enrichment and signal generation in complex biofluids, whereas concentration-normalized electroanalytical strategies address a central challenge in exosome assays by separating true biomarker abundance from variation in vesicle count ref [42], ref [43].

In vivo electrochemical sensing represents the most direct route to monitoring tumor-associated chemistry within living systems. Potentiometric and metabolically responsive platforms have been used to interrogate cancer-cell acidification behavior, as illustrated by pH-sensitive hydrogel nanofiber light-addressable potentiometric sensors for metabolic study ref [35]. Beyond ex vivo models, implanted or minimally invasive electrochemical probes have enabled real-time small-molecule measurements in awake, ambulatory animals, demonstrating the temporal resolution needed for dynamic tumor microenvironment studies ref [44]. This capability is exemplified by in vivo electrochemical detection of nitric oxide in tumor-bearing mice, which underscores the potential of electroanalytical devices to track reactive signaling molecules linked to angiogenesis, inflammation, and therapeutic response ref [45]. Together, cell-, exosome-, and in vivo-oriented platforms broaden electrochemical cancer biomarker analysis from static concentration measurement to systems-level phenotyping.

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Biosensor Platforms and Device Architectures
subsections.subsection_title: Nucleic Acid and Aptamer Sensor Devices
subsections.content:
Nucleic acid electrochemical sensors constitute a major platform for cancer biomarker analysis because they directly target sequence-specific DNA, methylated DNA, and noncoding RNAs with high molecular selectivity. Fundamental device designs typically rely on immobilized capture probes on Au, carbon, or microelectrode surfaces, where hybridization alters interfacial charge transfer, redox-tag position, or access of solution mediators to the electrode ref [49], ref [54]. Probe engineering strongly affects performance: peptide nucleic acids (PNAs) are especially attractive owing to their neutral backbone, high affinity, and superior mismatch discrimination, which improve hybridization efficiency in complex biofluids ref [50], ref [51]. Recent cancer-oriented examples include electrochemical assays for oral-cancer-related DNA and circulating methylated DNA, illustrating the translational relevance of sequence-specific electroanalysis ref [48], ref [57].

Signal generation in these devices spans label-free impedance/voltammetric readout and label-assisted strategies using transition-metal complexes or organic electroactive moieties ref [54]. To overcome the low abundance of circulating nucleic acid biomarkers, amplification modules such as rolling circle amplification (RCA) are frequently integrated with electrochemical transduction, enabling large local accumulation of redox reporters or catalytic nanomaterials ref [55]. Nanostructured interfaces further enhance sensitivity; for example, Pd nanoparticles have been used as both linkers and signal enhancers in label-free microRNA sensing ref [13]. Microelectrode-array formats have also enabled label-free electrical detection of exosomal microRNAs, supporting miniaturized and potentially multiplexed analysis of vesicle-associated cancer biomarkers ref [46].

Aptamer-based devices extend the nucleic-acid sensing paradigm from sequence recognition to folded affinity recognition of proteins, cells, and tumor-associated surface markers. Reviews have emphasized aptamers as versatile diagnostic ligands in cancer because they are chemically synthesized, readily modified with redox tags, and compatible with reagentless conformational switching architectures ref [52], ref [53]. In electrochemical implementations, target binding can modulate electron transfer through folding-induced distance changes, competitive displacement, or sandwich assembly, which is particularly suited to portable point-of-care formats. Representative studies such as an aptabiosensor for colon cancer diagnostics highlight the promise of aptamer electrodes for clinically relevant cancer screening workflows ref [47]. Together, DNA, PNA, microRNA, and aptamer devices provide a flexible architectural toolbox for highly selective electrochemical cancer biomarker detection.

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Detection and Monitoring of Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Electrochemical Detection of Circulating Tumor Cells
subsections.content:
Circulating tumor cells (CTCs) are clinically important but extremely rare, making their selective enrichment and sensitive quantification a central challenge for electrochemical biosensing. Recent reviews highlight that electrochemical CTC platforms couple affinity capture—most commonly through antibodies or aptamers against epithelial cell adhesion molecule (EpCAM) or related surface markers—with amperometric, voltammetric, or impedimetric readout to achieve compact, low-cost, and potentially point-of-care analysis ref [58]. Compared with optical methods, electrochemical schemes are attractive because they can be readily miniaturized, integrated with microfluidics, and adapted for label-free or signal-amplified detection.

A representative strategy uses nucleic-acid-assisted amplification after cell capture. In particular, rolling circle amplification (RCA) has been employed to convert CTC recognition into dense DNA products that generate amplified electrochemical current, substantially improving sensitivity for rare-cell analysis ref [2]. Such designs exemplify a broader trend in which nanoparticle tags, enzyme labels, redox-active probes, and DNA nanostructures are incorporated to boost signal output beyond that achievable by direct cell-electrode interactions alone ref [58], ref [2]. These amplification mechanisms are especially valuable in whole-blood contexts, where nonspecific adsorption and the low abundance of target cells otherwise limit performance.

Despite significant progress, important translational issues remain. Marker heterogeneity, particularly epithelial–mesenchymal transition-associated loss of EpCAM, can reduce capture efficiency, motivating multiplexed interfaces that combine antibodies, aptamers, or antifouling surfaces to improve robustness ref [58]. Future electrochemical CTC systems are therefore likely to emphasize integrated enrichment-detection architectures, multimarker recognition, and clinically validated operation in minimally processed blood samples, aligning CTC sensing with broader efforts in electrochemical monitoring of dynamic cancer models ref [58], ref [2].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Detection and Monitoring of Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Impedance-Based Monitoring of Cancer Cell Viability and Drug Response
subsections.content:
Impedance-based biosensing provides a label-free and non-destructive route to monitor cancer cell viability by tracking frequency-dependent changes in cell adhesion, spreading, membrane integrity, and barrier function at electrode interfaces. In practice, adherent tumor cells behave as insulating objects that modulate current pathways, so cytotoxic injury, detachment, or morphological remodeling can be resolved as real-time impedance signatures rather than endpoint viability readouts. This principle has been broadly established in cellular impedance biosensors for drug screening and toxin detection, which highlighted their utility for continuous pharmacodynamic profiling and kinetic discrimination between distinct modes of cell response ref [60].

Within cancer models, electrode architecture and surface chemistry strongly influence sensitivity. A representative example is the use of a multidisc indium tin oxide microelectrode array to quantify chitosan-induced cytotoxicity in MCF-7 breast cancer cells, where impedance analysis captured viability loss and time-dependent cell–substrate interactions with improved spatially distributed sensing ref [59]. Such studies illustrate how electrochemical impedance can resolve subtle treatment effects that may precede gross cell death, including reduced attachment, altered membrane capacitance, and changes in monolayer coverage. Compared with optical staining assays, impedance platforms are especially attractive for longitudinal monitoring because they minimize labels, repeated handling, and assay interruption ref [59], ref [60].

For anticancer drug response assessment, impedance traces can reveal dose-dependent kinetics, transient adaptation, and recovery after washout, enabling more informative evaluation than single time-point cytotoxicity tests ref [60]. This capability is particularly relevant for distinguishing cytostatic from cytotoxic effects and for integrating treatment response with engineered microenvironments in later-generation cancer models. Accordingly, impedance-based readouts are increasingly viewed as complementary to biochemical biomarkers, offering dynamic phenotyping of tumor-cell fitness that can be integrated with microelectrode arrays, organ-on-chip platforms, and multiplexed electrochemical sensing schemes ref [59], ref [60].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Detection and Monitoring of Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Redox and Hypoxia-Related Electrochemical Biomarkers in Cancer
subsections.content:
Redox dysregulation and hypoxia are tightly coupled hallmarks of malignant progression and therefore provide an important electrochemical window into tumor physiology. Cancer cells remodel reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, glutathione buffering, and compartment-specific redox signaling, while hypoxic adaptation stabilizes transcriptional programs that support angiogenesis, invasion, and therapy resistance ref [61], ref [64], ref [65]. Because many of these processes involve electroactive small molecules or redox-active enzymatic cascades, electrochemical biosensors are well suited for tracking tumor-associated oxidative stress in real time.

Among redox biomarkers, glutathione (GSH/GSSG balance), hydrogen peroxide, nitric oxide, and cellular redox potential have received the greatest attention. GSH is especially attractive because it is abundant, directly linked to antioxidant defense, and frequently elevated in drug-resistant tumors; recent nanostructure-based electrochemical sensors have improved its sensitivity and selectivity in complex biological environments ref [63]. At the cellular level, intracellular redox potential has also been linked to gene-regulatory changes under hypoxia, including altered miRNA expression in breast cancer cells, supporting the use of electrochemical redox readouts as functional biomarkers rather than merely metabolic byproducts ref [62].

Hypoxia-oriented electrochemical sensing further complements redox measurements by probing oxygen depletion, hypoxia-associated metabolites, or downstream adaptive responses. These signals are relevant not only for tumor identification but also for monitoring metastatic potential and treatment response, since hypoxic niches are associated with aggressiveness and reduced therapeutic efficacy ref [64], ref [65]. In engineered cancer models, integrating oxygen/redox electrodes with cell culture platforms can therefore enable longitudinal mapping of oxidative stress and hypoxic adaptation, offering a more mechanistic assessment of tumor state than endpoint biochemical assays alone ref [61], ref [63], ref [65].

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Detection and Monitoring of Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Integrated Sensor Platforms for Cancer Cell Culture Monitoring
subsections.content:
Integrated sensor platforms aim to move cancer cell culture analysis from endpoint assays toward continuous, multiplexed monitoring of the tumor microenvironment. In this context, sensorized culture vessels and microfluidic chips combine electrochemical transducers with standard cell-handling formats to track parameters such as pH, dissolved oxygen, impedance, and metabolite turnover in situ, thereby linking cellular phenotype with dynamic microenvironmental change rather than isolated biochemical snapshots ref [66], ref [67].

A representative example is the sensing cell culture flask, which embeds microsensors directly into a conventional flask architecture and enables noninvasive access to the pericellular environment during routine culture. Such designs are especially relevant for cancer models because they can reveal progressive acidification, oxygen depletion, and metabolic shifts associated with proliferation, stress adaptation, and treatment response without disturbing adherent cells ref [66]. By preserving compatibility with standard incubator workflows, these platforms also lower the barrier between biosensor development and biological adoption.

Microfluidic multi-sensor microsystems extend this concept by integrating transparent culture chambers with electrochemical and physicochemical sensing elements for parallel drug screening and time-resolved monitoring. The combination of optical accessibility and embedded sensors allows simultaneous observation of morphology and electrochemical signatures, which is valuable for distinguishing cytostatic from cytotoxic responses and for mapping heterogeneous responses across cancer cell populations ref [67]. More broadly, integrated platforms provide the technological basis for closed-loop, physiologically relevant cancer culture models in which environmental control, electrochemical readout, and longitudinal analysis are coupled within a single device architecture.

subsections.section_title: Electrochemical Detection and Monitoring of Cancer Models
subsections.subsection_title: Biosensing Interfaces in Engineered Cancer Models
subsections.content:
Biosensing interfaces are increasingly embedded into engineered cancer models to provide non-destructive, time-resolved readouts of microenvironmental state and tumor behavior. In tissue-engineered constructs, electrochemical and hybrid biosensors can be integrated with scaffolds, hydrogels, and microfluidic culture platforms to monitor pH, oxygen, metabolites, and secreted biomarkers without interrupting culture, thereby overcoming the endpoint bias of conventional staining or bulk biochemical assays ref [68]. For cancer modeling, this capability is especially important because engineered niches are dynamic and spatially heterogeneous, and sensor-compatible matrices can capture progressive changes in proliferation, invasion, and therapeutic adaptation under physiologically relevant transport conditions ref [68].

At the interface level, material selection and surface engineering govern both sensing performance and biological fidelity. Conductive polymers, carbon nanomaterials, and micro/nanoelectrode arrays have been used to improve signal transduction while preserving cell adhesion and matrix remodeling, whereas porous and soft substrates support three-dimensional growth closer to in vivo tumors ref [68]. In engineered cancer models, such interfaces are valuable when coupled to organoid, spheroid, or tumor-on-chip systems, where local gradients of oxygen and redox-active metabolites strongly influence malignant phenotype. Electrochemical interfaces can therefore be designed not only as detectors but also as functional culture substrates that resolve extracellular acidification, hypoxia-associated responses, and treatment-induced metabolic shifts in situ ref [68].

A key direction is the convergence of biosensing with advanced biofabrication. Sensor-integrated scaffolds and microphysiological systems permit multiplexed monitoring of viability, barrier function, and biochemical signaling over extended culture periods, which is critical for studying tumor–stroma interactions and personalized drug testing ref [68]. For surveying cancer biomarkers, these engineered interfaces are important because they translate complex 3D model behavior into quantifiable electrochemical outputs, helping bridge the gap between simplified cell assays and clinically relevant tumor microenvironments ref [68].

Illustrative figures in a review on electrochemical cancer-biomarker biosensors should do more than decorate the text; they should compress complex design choices into visually comparable modules. A useful opening figure is a taxonomy that maps clinically important targets—proteins, nucleic acids, exosomes, circulating tumor cells, and small-molecule metabolites—to the principal electrochemical transduction modes, including amperometry/voltammetry, impedance, potentiometry, and photoelectrochemistry, while also distinguishing affinity, enzymatic, and catalytic recognition strategies ref [69], ref [70], ref [71], ref [72], ref [73], ref [74]. Such a panel helps readers connect biomarker class with signal-generation logic and assay format.

A second category of figures should summarize representative sensing architectures. Schematics comparing antibody-, aptamer-, and molecularly imprinted interfaces; nanomaterial-enabled electrodes based on graphene, gold nanostructures, carbon nanotubes, metal oxides, and MXenes; and signal-amplification routes such as redox labels, enzyme tags, DNA walkers, hybridization chain reaction, and catalytic nanoparticles can efficiently convey structure–function relationships ref [75], ref [76], ref [77], ref [78], ref [79], ref [80], ref [81], ref [82], ref [83]. These figures are especially valuable when they standardize icons for immobilization chemistry, target capture, and electron-transfer pathways across different biomarker examples.

Performance-oriented figures are equally important. Comparative plots should benchmark limit of detection, linear range, assay time, sample matrix, and clinical validation depth for major biomarkers such as PSA, CEA, CA125, AFP, miRNAs, and exosomal markers, ideally using harmonized axes or bubble charts rather than isolated case studies ref [84], ref [85], ref [86], ref [87], ref [88]. A final translational figure can bridge laboratory innovation and deployment by illustrating workflows for multiplexed chips, microfluidic integration, wearable or point-of-care devices, and validation against standard immunoassays or molecular diagnostics ref [71], ref [74], ref [82], ref [88]. Together, such figures improve cross-study comparability and make the review more useful for both sensor developers and clinically oriented readers.
